ta-l1d26q2-d1e97.summary: The Prooemium of the second question of Distinction 26 turns to the properties and announces three articles: whether there are relations in God; whether the persons are distinguished by relations of origin alone; and the number of relations, notions, and properties and how they differ.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e109.summary: First argument that relations are nothing in God. Boethius says everything predicated of God becomes substance, but relation is not predicated at all, and whatever is in God is predicated of him.
claims: Relation is not predicated of God.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e112.summary: Second argument. Boethius says the relations of Father to Son and Son to Father are like those by which something is related to itself, as the same is the same as itself, and such relations posit nothing in reality, only in thought (the Philosopher).
claims: Divine relations resemble identity, a relation of reason.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e115.summary: Third argument. What comes to and leaves something only by another's relation to it, without its own change, posits nothing in it, since nothing can come to something anew without its change. Relations come and go this way, as a column becomes right or left by another's movement and a man stops being a father when his son dies.
claims: Relations come and go without change in their subject.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e119.summary: Fourth argument. A relation in God is either the same as the essence or other. If the same, being one in all, the relation would be one in all, or if the persons are distinguished by relations they would be distinguished in essence, Arius's heresy. If other, it would compose with the essence.
claims: Relation is either the essence or composes with it.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e122.summary: Fifth argument. The most simple are distinguished by themselves, and the divine persons are most simple, so they are not distinguished by relations.
claims: Simplest things distinguish themselves.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e125.summary: Sed contra. Everything in God is absolute or relative, and the persons are not distinguished in anything absolute, since in absolutes they are one. So they are either not distinguished or distinguished by relations, and if relations were only conceptual, Father and Son would not be really distinct, which is Sabellius's heresy.
claims: Without real relations Sabellianism follows.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e128.summary: Second sed contra. The Father is related to Son and Spirit in different ways, by begetting and by spirating, so several relations must be signified in one person, as several persons in one essence.
claims: Several relations in one person.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e131.summary: Thomas's determination. All Catholics agree there are relations in God but differ on how. The Porretans say they are only 'assisting'. Others say the relations are the persons themselves and are signified abstractly only by a manner of speech, as 'I ask your kindness' means 'you who are kind'. Others say the relations are the persons and also really in the persons, not only by manner of speech. All say something true, but the last contains the whole truth. In a relation, as in every accident, there is its being, by which it posits something in its subject, and its concept, by which it is referred to another and placed in its genus, and by this concept it does not posit something in its subject, as absolute forms do. So some relations posit nothing in their subject, and some philosophers concluded that relation is no genus of being and nothing in reality but a respect scattered through all beings, a second intention existing only in the soul, which the Porretan opinion seems to agree with. This is false, since nothing that is only in the soul is placed in a determinate genus. So relations must be distinguished: some have something in reality on which their being is founded, as equality on quantity, and are real; others have no foundation in the thing they are said of, as right and left in things without naturally determined positions (though in animals they are real, founded in the powers of parts), and these are relations of reason. A relation is of reason and not of reality in four ways: when it has no foundation in reality, so it may be real in one term and not the other, as all relations of God to creatures are real in the creature and not in God; when there is no real diversity between the terms, as identity; when it relates being to non-being, as our priority to those yet to be, since a real relation needs both terms in act; and when it is a relation of a relation, since a relation is related by itself (Avicenna gives the last two, and the first two can be drawn from the Philosopher). Since paternity and filiation have a foundation in reality, the nature communicated, they are really in God, by simplicity are the same as the persons in which they are, and by the truth of relation must be signified differently. The first opinion attended only to the 'toward another' of relations and not their foundation; the second to the foundation and divine simplicity; the third to both, saying the relations are in the persons by the true character of relation and are the persons by simplicity, as deity is in God and is God.
claims: Relations are really in God, founded on the communication of nature.
Relations are in the persons by the character of relation and are the persons by simplicity.
Relations of reason arise in four ways: no real foundation, no real diversity of terms, relation to non-being, relation of a relation.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e134.summary: Reply to the first argument. Boethius means relation as 'toward another', by which it does not predicate something in its subject but posits something outside, though some relations by their being do posit something in their subject.
claims: Relation by its esse can posit something in its subject.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e138.summary: Reply to the second argument. In a relation of identity there is that in respect of which identity is said, the essence, as equality in respect of quantity, and that whose identity it is, what is the same by one essence, as the equal has one quantity. Since the essence the Father communicates to the Son is numerically one, the divine relations resemble identity as to that in respect of which they are said, but not as to the terms related. So the Son is not called the same as (idem, masculine) the Father but the same (idem, neuter).
claims: Divine relations resemble identity only in their foundation, the one essence.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e141.summary: Reply to the third argument. When something of a thing's concept is removed, the thing is removed, as man without rational. Two things concur in a real relation: its foundation, e.g. quantity, its cause, and its respect to another. A real relation can be destroyed either by destroying the foundation, so a change in quantity brings an incidental change in relation, or by removing the term, so the relation ceases with no change in the related thing. So where there is relation only by this respect, relations come and go without change in what is related.
claims: Relations can cease by loss of foundation or of term.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e144.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Relation is really the same as the essence and differs only conceptually, as goodness does, and by that concept relation has the power to distinguish in God, which the essence does not.
claims: Relation is really the essence, distinct only conceptually, and distinguishes by its concept.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e147.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. The divine persons are distinguished by themselves inasmuch as they are really the relations, but as 'person' in mode of signifying is not the same as 'relation', they are not distinguished by themselves but by relations, as God is God by himself though deity is God, since he is his deity.
claims: Persons are distinguished by themselves in reality and by relations in mode of signifying.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e159.summary: First argument that relations of origin do not distinguish the hypostases. What conceptually follows the substance cannot be the principle of distinction among substances, and relation follows the substance in God, at least conceptually, like goodness and wisdom (Damascene).
claims: Relation follows the substance.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e162.summary: Second argument. The order of distinguishers should match the order of distinctions. The distinction of the divine persons is first among all distinctions, causing the procession of creatures (Dist. 14), and substance is first among beings, so its principle should be substance, not relation.
claims: The first distinction should have the first principle.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e165.summary: Third argument. Relation distinguishes only by opposition, which it has only as toward another, and as toward another it is not a thing, substance, or hypostasis, so it cannot make a real distinction of hypostases.
claims: As toward another, relation is no thing.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e169.summary: Fourth argument. There are many relations besides those of origin, like equality and likeness, so why do the persons distinguish only by those? If the others do not distinguish, for the same reason neither do these.
claims: Other relations exist in God.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e172.summary: Sed contra. The least distinction should have as principle what has least being and makes least composition, and relation has the weakest being (the Commentator), so much that some took it as a second intention.
claims: Relation has the weakest being.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e175.summary: Thomas's determination. Some say the principle of distinction is not relation, but the hypostases are distinguished by themselves through origin alone, with relations only manifesting the distinction, as properties in creatures manifest a numerical difference caused by division of matter. This cannot be: things distinguished by themselves have in their concepts some ground of distinction, as substance and quantity by being subsistent and being a measure, but two hypostases as hypostases have nothing in their concept to distinguish them, so they need some determination, either determinate matter, impossible in God, or something else. If that is origin, either origin means the relation of origin, which is the view defended, or origin as an operation, which does not distinguish hypostases but presupposes them distinct, since operations belong to distinct individuals (the Philosopher). So the only principle of distinction in God is relation. All distinction or division is by quantity or by form; there is no quantity or matter in God; and every formal distinction rests on some opposition, broadly taken, including perfect and imperfect. In every opposition one term is perfect and the other imperfect, except relation: this is plain in affirmation and negation and in privation and habit, and in contrariety one contrary is always nobler and the other baser and like a privation. So no such distinction can be in God, who is wholly perfect. In relatives neither is the privation of the other or implies defect, since relative opposition concerns not what the relative is in something but what it is toward another. Although one relation carries a negation of the other in the same supposit, this negation implies no defect, which concerns only what something is naturally apt to have, so only relative opposition suits the distinction of persons.
claims: Relation is the only principle of distinction in God; origin as operation presupposes distinction.
Only relative opposition involves no imperfection in either term, so only it suits God.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e178.summary: Reply to the first argument. A divine relation has something as relation and something as divine. As divine it is a subsistent hypostasis, since there is nothing accidental or non-subsistent inhering form there. Though it does not distinguish hypostases simply as relation, since then every relation would, it does as divine relation, and so it does not follow the substance but is the substance.
claims: As divine, relation is the substance and a subsistent hypostasis.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e181.summary: Reply to the second argument. The order of distinction can be taken by its quantity or by its dignity and causality. By quantity, the distinction of the divine hypostases is the least real distinction possible, so the least being, relation, fits it. By dignity and causality it excels all distinctions, and so does relation as its principle, not as relation but as divine relation, excelling all distinguishers in creatures in dignity and in causality, since from the procession of distinct divine persons all procession and multiplication of creatures is caused (Dist. 14).
claims: The divine distinction is least in quantity but highest in dignity and causality.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e184.summary: Reply to the third argument. Although, as toward another, relation is not owed being a thing, it is a thing by having a foundation in what is related, and further, as divine, it is a hypostasis or substance, so it makes a real distinction of hypostases, as wisdom is not substance as wisdom, yet God is substantially wise because divine wisdom is substance. Where there is relation only by respect and not by natural being, a distinction of supposits is required only conceptually ('the same is the same as itself'); where there is relation by natural being, a real distinction of supposits is required ('the equal is equal to the equal'); and where the relation is not only real but is the substance of the related, it does not just require but makes the distinction of supposits.
claims: Relation by foundation is a thing, and as divine it is a hypostasis.
A divine relation, being the substance of the related, makes the distinction of supposits.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e188.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Relation has natural being only from its foundation, which places it in a genus, so the essential differences of relations follow the differences of other beings (some founded on quantity, some on action, the Philosopher), and the order of relations follows the order of their foundations. As in things distinguished by essence the principles of substance, matter and form, distinguish while accidents are signs manifesting the distinction, so among things distinguished by relation, the relations founded on the nature distinguish and the others are signs. The relations founded on the nature are relations of origin, since paternity is founded on communication of nature, so the saints say Father and Son are distinguished by paternity and filiation, while equality and likeness show the distinction, as Hilary proved the distinction from likeness (Dist. 25).
claims: Relations of origin, founded on the nature communicated, distinguish; equality and likeness only manifest distinction.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e200.summary: First argument that there are more than five notions. What arises in something only from another's relation to it is multiplied by the number of things related to it, since plurality of causes yields plurality of effects, so there are as many relations in God as creatures related to him.
claims: Relations multiply with their terms.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e203.summary: Second argument. According to Augustine the ideas of things to be created were in God from eternity, differing only by relations to creatures, so there are as many relations as creatures whose ideas are in God.
claims: Ideas differ by relations to creatures.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e206.summary: Third argument. The divine persons are compared not only by the nature one receives from another but by other attributes, with relations of equality or likeness, so there are as many relations as attributes.
claims: Attributes yield relations of equality and likeness.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e210.summary: Fourth argument. Every operation gives rise to a relation of the agent to its object, and several operations are distinguished in God conceptually, willing, understanding, and so on. As relations of origin follow generation, others would follow these, knower to known and willer to willed, multiplying relations with operations.
claims: Each operation yields a relation.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e213.summary: Fifth argument. As Father and Son agree in being principle of the Spirit, Son and Spirit agree in being from the Father as principle, so as common spiration is a relation common to Father and Son, 'being from the Father' would be another relation common to Son and Spirit, making more than five.
claims: 'Being from the Father' would be a sixth notion.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e216.summary: Contrary argument that there are fewer. The properties are subsistent persons (previous article), so there are as many properties as subsisting persons, only three.
claims: Properties are as many as persons.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e219.summary: Thomas's determination. The difference of notion, property, and relation can be assigned in three ways. By signification: paternity is called relation as referred to the Son, property as belonging to the Father alone, and notion as the formal principle of making the Father known. By order of understanding: nothing makes something known unless proper to it, so property precedes notion; and since a property belongs only to something distinct, and distinction in God is only by relative opposition, relation precedes property. By number: there are five notions, paternity, filiation, procession, innascibility, and common spiration. Four are properties, belonging to one person: paternity and innascibility to the Father, filiation to the Son, procession to the Spirit. Common spiration is a property only in some respect, proper to Father and Son with respect to the Spirit. Four are relations: paternity, filiation, procession, and common spiration; innascibility is a relation only by reduction, as negation is reduced to the genus of affirmation. Three are personal, constituting the persons like constitutive differences: paternity, filiation, procession; the other two are properties of persons but not personal. The sufficiency of the five follows from three conditions for a notion: it pertains to origin, since the persons are distinguished by relations of origin; to dignity, since a person is a hypostasis distinguished by a property of dignity; and is special, since the common does not make known. What pertains to origin is signified affirmatively or negatively. Affirmatively, as principle ('from whom another') or as from a principle ('who is from another'), both common, so neither is a notion; they must be determined to the special modes of origin, which are only two, by nature and by love (Dist. 13), each giving a principle-relation and a from-principle relation: paternity and filiation for nature, common spiration and procession for love. Negatively, either the principle-character is denied, which pertains to no dignity and so cannot be the Spirit's notion, or the from-principle character is denied, specially or generally. Denied specially it is not a notion, since the more special an affirmation the more common its negation ('non-man' is more common than 'non-animal'). Denied generally it is a special negation pertaining to dignity, and gives the Father's notion, innascibility, not being from another; why it is named by privation of birth is treated in Dist. 28.
claims: Relation, property, and notion differ in signification and order: relation precedes property, which precedes notion.
There are five notions; four properties; four relations; three personal properties.
The five are derived from origin, by nature and love, as principle or from principle, plus innascibility as general negation of being from another.
concepts: modes of origin: nature and love

ta-l1d26q2-d1e222.summary: Reply to the first argument. Relations signified in God from creatures' relation to him posit nothing really in God (Article 1), so real relations in God are not multiplied infinitely.
claims: God's relations to creatures are of reason.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e225.summary: Reply to the second argument. The relations by which the ideas are distinguished are founded not in the divine being but in his intellect, so they have no real being in God but are only understood by him, like the form of an ass or a horse, and not as goodness and wisdom have being in him.
claims: Relations distinguishing the ideas are only in God's understanding.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e229.summary: Reply to the third argument. Equality and likeness add no real relation to paternity and filiation, for reasons given in Dist. 31.
claims: Equality and likeness add no real relations.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e232.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. A relation not underlain by real distinction in the related is not a real relation, so when an operation reflects back on the operating supposit, no real relation arises, only one of reason; so 'God (or the soul) understands himself' implies no real relation.
claims: Reflexive operations yield only relations of reason.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e235.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. 'Being from another' does not name a determinate mode of origin, so it is no special notion; it is preserved in filiation and procession and is not counted with them, as a common is not counted with the propers under it. Common spiration names a determinate mode of origin, by which Father and Son are principle of the Spirit, so it is a special notion.
claims: Being from another is common and not a notion; common spiration is determinate.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e238.summary: Reply to the sixth argument. Every property in God, and everything there, is subsistent, but there are not as many subsistent things as properties, only as many as really distinguishing opposition requires. As goodness and wisdom are subsistent but not different subsistents, lacking opposition, common spiration is subsistent but not another subsistent from paternity and filiation, not being opposed to them, so it can be in one subsistent with each. It does not constitute the person it is in, since by order of nature it presupposes paternity and filiation, as procession presupposes generation, so it is not a personal notion. Innascibility, not opposed to paternity, can be in the same subsistent, and since its negation follows conceptually the positing of principle, it does not constitute a person but is in the person constituted by paternity.
claims: Only opposed properties make distinct subsistents.
Common spiration and innascibility are not personal, since they presuppose the constituted persons.

ta-l1d26q2-d1e248.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'Nothing is said by accident' seems to fail, since there are inseparable accidents, but every subject can be understood without its accident, while the supposit of a relation cannot be understood without the relation, since the relation is the subsisting supposit, so it is not an accident; every accident involves composition with its subject and so mutability, since the composite is divisible. (2) 'All men are sons of God by making' means by creation, though only what is in the image has the name of sonship; or better, by adoption, since a man becomes a son who was not, and not by origin of birth like the eternal Son (III, Dist. 10). (3) 'Nor anything properly but Son' because filiation is his whole substance, which does not exclude the divine essence, since the essence in the Son is filiation. (4) 'By origin, not adoption' is against Nestorius and Photinus, who made God and the man different persons, so the son of man would be Son of God by adoption; 'in truth, not by name' is against Sabellius, who denied any real distinction under 'Father' and 'Son'; 'by birth, not creation' against Arius, who made the Son a creature. The rest is clear from Dist. 18 on the Holy Spirit.
claims: Divine relations are not accidents, since the supposit cannot be understood without them.
The Son is Son by origin, in truth, and by birth, against Nestorius, Sabellius, and Arius.

ta-l1d26q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium announces three articles on the properties: whether there are relations in God, whether relations of origin alone distinguish the persons, and the number and difference of relations, notions, and properties.

ta-l1d26q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 holds that relations are really in God. Distinguishing a relation's being from its concept 'toward another', Thomas rejects the view that relation is only a second intention and sets out four ways a relation is merely of reason, including God's relations to creatures. Paternity and filiation are real, founded on the communication of nature. Of three opinions (Porretan assisting relations; relations as the persons by manner of speech; relations both in and identical with the persons), the third holds the whole truth: they are in the persons by the character of relation and are the persons by simplicity. Relation is really the essence, distinct only conceptually, and the divine relations resemble identity only in their foundation.
claims: Relations are really in God, founded on the communication of nature, and are both in and identical with the persons.
Relations of reason arise in four ways.

ta-l1d26q2-Dd1e151.summary: Article 2 holds that relation is the only principle of distinction in God, against those who make origin, taken as operation, distinguish the hypostases. Formal distinction rests on opposition, and only relative opposition involves no imperfection in either term. As divine, relation is the substance and a subsistent hypostasis, so it makes, not just requires, the distinction of supposits. The divine distinction is least in quantity but highest in dignity and causality. Relations of origin, founded on the nature communicated, distinguish, while equality and likeness only manifest the distinction.
claims: Only relations of origin distinguish the divine persons.
Relative opposition alone involves no imperfection.

ta-l1d26q2-Dd1e192.summary: Article 3 distinguishes relation, property, and notion by signification and order of understanding (relation, then property, then notion), and holds that there are five notions: paternity, filiation, procession, innascibility, and common spiration. Of these, four are properties, four are relations, and three are personal. The five are derived from origin by nature and by love, as principle or from principle, plus innascibility as general negation of being from another. Relations to creatures and among the ideas are of reason, equality and likeness add no real relations, reflexive operations yield no real relations, and only opposed properties make distinct subsistents.
claims: There are five notions, four properties, four relations, and three personal properties.
Only opposed properties constitute distinct subsistents.

ta-l1d26q2-Dd1e243.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 26, question 2, explains that divine relations are not accidents, since their supposit cannot be understood without them, distinguishes creaturely and adoptive sonship from the eternal Son's, and reads Lombard's formulas as directed against Nestorius, Photinus, Sabellius, and Arius.
claims: Divine relations are not accidents.
The Son is Son by origin, truly, and by birth.

ta-l1d26q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 26 treats the divine properties. Article 1 holds that relations are really in God, founded on the communication of nature, distinguishing real relations from four kinds of relations of reason and holding that the divine relations are both in the persons and identical with them. Article 2 holds that relation, specifically relation of origin, is the only principle of distinction in God, since only relative opposition is free of imperfection and divine relation is itself the subsistent substance. Article 3 orders relation, property, and notion and establishes five notions, four properties, four relations, and three personal properties.
claims: Relations are really in God and identical with the persons.
Relations of origin alone distinguish the persons.
There are five notions, three of them personal.
